candidates.name: Dora
candidates.description: Dora (Dataflow-Oriented Robotic Architecture) is middleware for composing AI-based robotic applications as low-latency, distributed dataflow pipelines.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate; ADR 023 role test
triage.finding: Ships an installable CLI (cargo install dora-cli) and Python API (pip install dora-rs) with releases, CI, and a public node hub, so a maintained run path is documented. Its documented outcome is a declarative dataflow graph: the node hub lists ready-made nodes for cameras, YOLO, LLMs, and TTS, and the README documents a ROS2 bridge carrying 'bidirectional topics, services, and actions over DDS' between graph nodes and ROS2, where 'actions' is the ROS2 request/feedback/result concept rather than actuation. The README never uses the words actuator, hardware, physical, or VLM, so a model node's output reaching a robot's actuator through this bridge is a reasonable inference from what a ROS2-connected dataflow graph does, not a claim the README makes outright. No existing role names composing a dataflow graph that mixes model node types (LLM, YOLO) with a ROS2 bridge to robot software; the node-hub and LLM-node claims are stated directly in the README's feature list without reading the source tree, but the actuator link is not.

candidates.name: Figure
candidates.description: Figure is an AI robotics company building a general-purpose humanoid robot for commercial deployment.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate condition 4
triage.finding: figure.ai is served through a Vercel CDN edge cache: repeated fetches within a single verification session return identical bytes with a constant ETag and a climbing 'age' header (observed on the terms-and-conditions, privacy-policy, accessibility-statement, and home pages alike), so the site reads as stable while any one review is underway. But a shared footer icon component embeds a randomly generated SVG gradient identifier that is baked in at origin render time; that value changes only when the edge cache invalidates and Vercel re-renders from origin on its own stale-while-revalidate cadence, not on every request. That makes a hash pinned to any figure.ai page unsafe to rely on indefinitely -- it can hold for an entire review session and still not survive to a later recheck once the cache regenerates, which is exactly the failure this review hit once already when a Wayback capture of this same page was hashed moments after being triggered and had not yet settled. The terms-and-conditions page was read live: it is a generic website Terms and Conditions, dated February 2023 in its own body text, governing use of figure.ai itself (account access, electronic communications, linked sites) with no mention of the robot as a product, its sale, its licensing, or its onboard software, and no product page publishes a price or purchase path. That reading is a first-party observation, not a durably re-verifiable citation, for the CDN-cache reason above; the site's own sitemap is cited instead because, as a static file with no templated component, it does not carry the same regeneration risk, and it establishes from a stable first-party source that the terms page exists and when Figure's content system last touched it. No product-specific terms or licence establishing a reviewed source model and complete licence list are published on any first-party page, and no page on the domain carrying that content can be durably pinned for a checkable citation in the first place.

evidence.label: Sitemap (the only figure.ai resource found to be byte-stable across repeated fetches; it confirms the terms-and-conditions URL exists but carries no terms content itself)

candidates.name: urdfdom
candidates.description: urdfdom is the reference parser library for URDF (Unified Robot Description Format), the XML format ROS uses to describe a robot's kinematic and visual structure.

triage.rule: docs/SPECIFICATIONS.md inclusion boundary
triage.finding: Reviewable unit is a specification: URDF, a versioned XML vocabulary for a robot's kinematic and visual structure, whose reference parser this repo also ships. This repo's own README states plainly, 'For now, the details of the URDF specifications reside on http://ros.org/wiki/urdf' -- the parser repository disclaims being the format's authoritative documentation home. I followed that link (it redirects to https://wiki.ros.org/urdf) and read two things there: the page carries the ROS project's own end-of-life banner stating 'the ROS Wiki (this website) will also be EOL and transition to being an archive' and directing 'Maintainers: Please migrate any wiki content into your package's README.md file,' and its body already states 'The core URDF parser and data structures (urdfdom, urdfdom_headers) have been pushed upstream into stand alone (no ROS-dependencies) software packages' -- naming this repo by name as where that content now lives. That supports reading urdfdom's README, not the wiki, as the format's current documentation surface, consistent with the versioned 1.0/1.1/1.2 attribute table the README itself carries (exact required and optional attributes, numeric defaults, and forward/backward parsing compatibility for each geometry and joint-limit feature) -- real normative detail, satisfying docs/SPECIFICATIONS.md's normative-detail requirement without reading any source file. The wiki page was read but not pinned as evidence: it is an archive-bound third-party page -- EOL by its own banner, which directs its content into package READMEs -- rather than the format's maintained authoritative home. What this paragraph reports of that page's content is what I read there, not verified first-party evidence the way the pinned README and LICENSE are. URDF is not caught by the boundary's refusal sentence: it is not a general transport, a general serialization format, or an API description language -- it is a domain-specific vocabulary for one thing, a robot's structure, the same way an admitted metadata schema is a domain-specific vocabulary rather than a generic encoding. It also does not cleanly fit the admission sentence: the contract's boundary connects a physical robot's description to the software that consumes it (parsers, simulators, motion planners). The closest of the ten specification_scopes is tool_data_integration ('Connects model applications to tools, resources, prompts, and external data'), since a URDF file is exactly the kind of external data a downstream tool consumes, but it fails to name that the entity described is a physical robot -- hardware -- rather than a model application, tool, resource, or prompt in the software sense. None of the ten specification_scopes values, and none of the boundary parties docs/SPECIFICATIONS.md enumerates (agents, tools, clients, users, repositories, extension packages), name a robot or hardware description boundary; admitting this record would require a scope identifier that does not exist today, and ADR 017 ties that extension to the change that admits a record, not to this sweep. Identity caution for a future reviewer: this candidate's repo and url fields point at the parser (ros/urdfdom, github.com/ros/urdfdom), not at a specification home. If URDF is ever promoted to directory/specifications.json, resolve first where the format's own current authoritative documentation actually lives -- the README's cited wiki page is itself EOL and being archived, and I did not verify what, if anything, has replaced it as URDF's canonical home -- before assuming this repo's url is the right one to record, the way an admitted record points at a specification's own home rather than at one implementation of it.

candidates.name: BabyAGI (functionz)
candidates.description: The maintainer's active, differently-scoped project now published under the BabyAGI name and repository: a 'functionz' framework for registering, storing, and executing Python functions from a database, with dependency tracking, secrets handling, and a management dashboard. Distinct in architecture and outcome from the original 2023 task-loop BabyAGI, which the maintainer moved to yoheinakajima/babyagi_archive (published separately as `babyagi`). setup.py claims the MIT License but the repository ships no LICENSE file, so source terms remain unresolved.

triage.rule: docs/CURATION.md inclusion gate condition 4; ADR 016 and ADR 020
triage.finding: No LICENSE file could be fetched (HTTP 404); the bundle contains only a README, which makes no license statement. The README states this "newest BabyAGI" superseded the original March-2023 project (now archived separately) and describes "an experimental framework for a self-building autonomous agent," with a core "functionz" framework for registering, loading, and executing functions from a database, a dependency graph with automatic loading, a management dashboard, and two experimental self-building agents that generate and register new functions from natural-language task descriptions. The maintainer's own caution is explicit: "This is a framework built by Yohei who has never held a job as a developer... Not meant for production use." It installs as a real PyPI package (`pip install babyagi`). The bundle reports no cross-collection hits. Boundary question: no license evidence exists in this bundle to review, and a reviewer will need to weigh the maintainer's own "not meant for production use" caution against the genuine working engine (dashboard, logging, triggers, self-building agents) documented here.
